data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms strictly as a non-inductive, critical choice to act on the theory that has withstood the most severe tests so far, accepting the cost that this preference offers no rational guarantee of future success and explicitly rejects the notion that corroboration increases the probability of truth.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent requires a probabilistic guarantee that the preferred theory will succeed in the next instance, the Popperian defense fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'preference' is interpreted as assigning a higher degree of belief or logical probability to the theory, the defense collapses into the induction Popper rejected.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the choice between two unfalsified theories cannot be grounded in the severity of tests they have faced (e.g., if both are equally untested), the mechanism provides no guidance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Critical Rational Choice via Severe Testing: The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification' (which implies induction/probability) and 'criticism' (which implies selection based on falsifiability). A scientist prefers Theory A over Theory B not because A is likely true, but because B has been falsified or A has survived tests that would have falsified it if it were false. This is a decision to adopt the best available error-eliminated option for action, treating corroboration as a report of past performance rather than a predictor of future reliability.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
